1081.event: In 1274 the young Dante Alighieri, about nine years old, first saw Beatrice Portinari, a girl of about the same age, at her father's house in Florence. In his book La Vita Nuova he later described how she appeared dressed in modest red and how the sight overwhelmed him, so that from then on love ruled his soul. Beatrice married another man and died in 1290, and she became the guiding figure of his Divine Comedy.
1081.explanation: Dante's account of this first sight became one of the most famous descriptions of love at first sight in world literature.
1081.tie_back: Like the hero of the kural who cannot tell whether he has seen a goddess or a human girl, Dante wrote of Beatrice as a heavenly presence from the moment he first saw her.
1081._accuracy_note: A very close match to the kural's bewildered first sight, though our knowledge of the meeting comes mainly from Dante's own poetic account.

1082.event: The Italian poet Petrarch recorded in a note in his copy of Virgil that he first saw the woman he called Laura on 6 April 1327 in Avignon, in the church of Sainte-Claire. He wrote hundreds of love poems to her, collected in his Canzoniere. In the same note he recorded that she died in Avignon on 6 April 1348.
1082.explanation: Petrarch's poems to Laura shaped the love sonnet for centuries across Europe.
1082.tie_back: The kural describes the overwhelming force of the beloved's returning glance; a single sight of Laura in church captured Petrarch for the rest of his life.
1082._accuracy_note: A strong example of a single meeting of eyes conquering the lover, but the sources do not record that Laura returned his look, which is the kural's exact image.

1083.event: The poet John Keats met Fanny Brawne in late 1818, and in April 1819 she moved into the other half of Wentworth Place in Hampstead, next door to him. They became secretly engaged, and he wrote her passionate letters. In February 1820 a lung haemorrhage convinced Keats he was dying of tuberculosis, and he died in Rome in February 1821, aged 25, without being able to marry her.
1083.explanation: Their love letters are among the most famous in English and show love and mortal illness bound together.
1083.tie_back: The kural's lover says he has now learned what Death is, for it has a woman's grace; for Keats, love for Fanny and the approach of death arrived together.
1083._accuracy_note: Love and death are joined in Keats's story, but the kural's image of the beloved's eyes as Death itself is a figure of speech, so the fit is partial.

1084.event_title: Vermeer paints Girl with a Pearl Earring
1084.event: Around 1665 Johannes Vermeer painted a young woman in a turban and a large pearl earring, turning to look out at the viewer with her lips softly parted. The Mauritshuis in The Hague explains that it is a tronie, a study of an imaginary figure rather than a portrait of a named person. Its simple setting, light and direct gaze have made it one of the most recognised paintings in the world.
1084.explanation: The painting shows how a gentle, quiet figure can hold every viewer through the power of a look.
1084.tie_back: The kural speaks of a gentle, innocent girl whose eyes seem to seize all who see them; Vermeer's quiet young woman draws in viewers above all through her gaze.
1084._accuracy_note: Captures the contrast between a gentle figure and a powerful gaze, but it is a painting rather than a lived love story.

1085.event_title: Leonardo da Vinci paints the Mona Lisa
1085.place: Florence, Italy (now in the Louvre, Paris)
1085.event: Leonardo da Vinci began the portrait known as the Mona Lisa in Florence around 1503 and continued working on it for years; it is now in the Louvre. The sitter is traditionally identified as Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine merchant Francesco del Giocondo. Her enigmatic smile and expression, painted with Leonardo's soft sfumato shading, have been studied and debated for centuries.
1085.explanation: It is probably the most famous painting in the world, largely because viewers cannot settle on what her expression means.
1085.tie_back: The kural's lover sees several natures in one young woman's look at once; the Mona Lisa's expression is famous for seeming to hold more than one meaning at the same time.
1085._accuracy_note: Shows a single look holding several natures at once, but it does not show the kural's specific mix of danger, beauty and doe-like shyness.

1086.event_title: Frida Kahlo paints Diego on My Mind
1086.event: In 1943, a few years after she and Diego Rivera remarried in 1940, Frida Kahlo painted Diego on My Mind (Self-Portrait as Tehuana). She shows herself in a Tehuana headdress of starched lace framing her face, with a small portrait of Rivera placed on her forehead just above her dark, joined eyebrows. The painting is now in the Jacques and Natasha Gelman Collection.
1086.explanation: The work is a famous image of a love so consuming that the beloved occupies the painter's very brow and thoughts.
1086.tie_back: The kural dwells on the beloved's brow and eyes as the source of the lover's trouble; Kahlo set her husband's image on her own forehead, between her brows, to show how he filled her mind.
1086._accuracy_note: Brows, eyes and love meet in this image, but the kural's wish that the curved brows would hide the eyes is not illustrated.

1087.event_title: Draperies are painted over Michelangelo's Last Judgment
1087.event: In 1564, after the Council of Trent, church authorities decided that some figures in Michelangelo's Last Judgment fresco in the Sistine Chapel were improper and should be covered. The work of painting draperies over them was given to Michelangelo's follower Daniele da Volterra, who was nicknamed Il Braghettone, the breeches-maker. Encyclopaedia Britannica dates his commission to 1559 under Pope Paul IV.
1087.explanation: The episode is a well-known example of cloth being added to cover a powerful image whose effect authorities feared.
1087.tie_back: The kural compares a garment over the beloved to the cloth over a raging elephant's face, a covering meant to hold a dangerous power in check; the draperies were added for the same kind of reason.
1087._accuracy_note: The idea of cloth restraining a dangerous beauty matches, but the setting is religious art, not love; the sources also differ on the year (1559 or 1564).

1088.event_title: Napoleon's love letters to Josephine from Italy
1088.event: Napoleon Bonaparte married Josephine de Beauharnais in March 1796 and days later left to command the French army in Italy. While winning battles there, he wrote her frequent, passionate letters begging her to join him and complaining that she rarely wrote back. Josephine preferred to stay in Paris for several months.
1088.explanation: The letters show the general who was conquering Italy as helpless and pleading in love.
1088.tie_back: The kural's warrior laments that strength which made enemies tremble has broken before one woman's brow; Napoleon, victorious in the field, wrote to Josephine as a man at her mercy.
1088._accuracy_note: A strong match of a feared commander undone by love, though Napoleon's might as a general was not actually broken.

1089.event: When Marie Sklodowska married Pierre Curie in July 1895, they held a simple civil ceremony with no religious service, and they did not exchange rings. Instead of a white bridal gown she wore a dark blue outfit, chosen so that she could wear it afterwards in the laboratory.
1089.explanation: The wedding is remembered as a sign of the Curies' simplicity and their devotion to each other and to their work.
1089.tie_back: The kural asks what use ornaments are to one who already has natural grace and modesty; Marie Curie married without a gown or rings and needed neither.
1089._accuracy_note: A clear example of a bride who did without ornament, though the kural's point is about her natural beauty while the sources stress practicality.

1090.event_title: Shah Jahan builds the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal
1090.event: After his wife Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan ordered a great white marble mausoleum built in her memory at Agra. Construction ran from 1631 to 1648, and both of them are buried there. UNESCO, which listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1983, calls it one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage.
1090.explanation: The Taj Mahal is the world's best-known monument to love, admired by people who never knew the couple.
1090.tie_back: The kural says love, unlike strong drink, delights even those who only look; the love behind the Taj Mahal still moves the countless visitors who simply look at it.
1090._accuracy_note: Fits the idea of love delighting onlookers, though the kural speaks of the joy of seeing the beloved rather than a monument.
